[LLM] Outbound fetch of attacker-controlled autoimport VSIX from ColossusQuailPray GitHub release Delivery High
Detects the GlassWorm second-stage payload download: the Zig dropper fetches autoimport-2.7.9.vsix from https://github.com/ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde/releases/download/12/ to /tmp before silently installing it into every IDE. Both the GitHub username and the file path are uniquely attributed to this campaign. Rationale: The full URL `https://github.com/ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde/releases/download/12/autoimport-2.7.9.vsix` is published in the article's IOC list; both the GitHub user `ColossusQuailPray` and the VSIX filename `autoimport-2.7.9.vsix` are unique campaign artifacts with no legitimate use, giving an essentially zero-FP signal. We also pivot through DeviceFileEvents.FileOriginUrl so the same indicator is caught even when SSL inspection is missing. Corroborated by THN and SecurityAffairs which both restate the GitHub release URL. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/glassworm-campaign-uses-zig-dropper-to.html • https://securityaffairs.com/190638/malware/glassworm-evolves-with-zig-dropper-to-infect-multiple-developer-tools.html • https://www.scworld.com/brief/glassworm-uses-zig-binary-to-infect-multiple-ides
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002 T1102.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
union
  ( DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde", "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, ActionType ),
  ( DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix" or FileOriginUrl has_any ("ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde", "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, RemoteUrl = FileOriginUrl, ActionType )
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  ( ImWebSession
      | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
      | where Url has_any ("ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde", "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix")
      | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent ),
  ( CommonSecurityLog
      | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
      | where RequestURL has_any ("ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde", "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix")
      | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication ),
  ( ImFileEvent
      | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
      | where TargetFileName =~ "autoimport-2.7.9.vsix"
      | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GlassWorm Second-Stage Autoimport VSIX Download From Attacker GitHub Release
id: a0e1c7d2-4f6e-4b3c-9a72-2c8f6b4d3e10
status: experimental
description: Detects the GlassWorm Zig dropper fetching its second-stage extension autoimport-2.7.9.vsix from the attacker-controlled GitHub repository ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde. The URL path and GitHub user are exclusively attributed to this campaign by Aikido and corroborated by The Hacker News.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/glassworm-zig-dropper-infects-every-ide-on-your-machine
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/glassworm-campaign-uses-zig-dropper-to.html
  - https://securityaffairs.com/190638/malware/glassworm-evolves-with-zig-dropper-to-infect-multiple-developer-tools.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/13
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1102.001
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde'
      - 'autoimport-2.7.9.vsix'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - None expected — the GitHub username and VSIX filename are uniquely tied to this campaign.
level: high
(@http.url:(*ColossusQuailPray\/oiegjqde* OR *autoimport-2.7.9.vsix*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:*github.com* @CommandLine:*ColossusQuailPray*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Code.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe) @DestinationHostname:*github*)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde*" OR Web.url="*autoimport-2.7.9.vsix*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde*" OR Web.url="*autoimport-2.7.9.vsix*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.user Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com/ColossusQuailPray/oiegjqde")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);

ImNetworkSession

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or SHA1 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or MD5 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or SHA1 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44") or MD5 in~ ("2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2819ea44e22b9c47049e86894e544f3fd0de1d8afc7b545314bd3bc718bf2e02", "112d1b33dd9b0244525f51e59e6a79ac5ae452bf6e98c310e7b4fa7902e4db44"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft via localhost.* / sslip.io bypass Exploitation High
Hunts requests to Hoppscotch's /device-login endpoint where the redirect_uri parameter abuses the flawed startsWith('http://localhost') validation by using localhost.<attacker-domain> or localhost.<ip>.sslip.io to exfiltrate session tokens. Detects GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the exact bypass primitives the article documents: redirect_uri=http://localhost.<attacker>/ and the sslip.io payload (http://localhost.<attacker-ip>.sslip.io/) the Aikido agents used to verify the flaw. The startsWith('http://localhost') check passes any subdomain of an attacker-controlled domain — these two substrings are the highest-fidelity signal because legitimate device-login uses bare http://localhost/device-token. Cross-referenced GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v and PR #6012. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6012 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10462
ATT&CKT1539 T1190 T1566.002

| where RemoteUrl contains "/device-login"
| where RemoteUrl contains "redirect_uri"
| where RemoteUrl contains "localhost." or RemoteUrl contains "sslip.io"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem contains "/device-login"
| where csUriQuery contains "redirect_uri"
| where csUriQuery contains "localhost." or csUriQuery contains "sslip.io"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csUserName, scStatus
title: Hoppscotch device-login open redirect token theft

description: Detects requests to Hoppscotch /device-login with redirect_uri pointing to localhost.* subdomains or sslip.io patterns, exploiting GHSA-7fg7-wx5q-6m3v in versions <= 2026.2.1.

[LLM] Hoppscotch Mock Server stored XSS via GraphQL updateRESTUserRequest content-type override Exploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL traffic invoking the updateRESTUserRequest mutation with a response body that sets Content-Type:text/html and embeds script-bearing markup, then correlates with subsequent GET requests to /mock/<subdomain>/ from the same client. Detects GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation against versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Targets the exact mutation name the article cites (updateRESTUserRequest) plus the malicious payload shape — a response header object with key:content-type and value:text/html paired with an XSS-bearing body (<img src=x onerror=...>). The Sentinel query uses a same-source-IP correlation between a /graphql POST and a subsequent /mock/ GET because Hoppscotch's mock URLs sit at /mock/<subdomain>/ and rendering them is what triggers the planted script. WAF body inspection (Datadog @http.body) gives the cleanest single-event signal. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v and PR #6006. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/hoppscotch/hoppscotch/pull/6006 • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10463
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
let GraphqlPosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains "/graphql"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","python.exe","node.exe")
    | project GraphqlTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName, GraphqlUrl=RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "/mock/"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe")
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project Timestamp, GraphqlTime, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, MockUrl=RemoteUrl, GraphqlUrl
let GraphqlPosts = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem contains "/graphql"
    | where csMethod == "POST"
    | project GraphqlTime=TimeGenerated, GraphqlIP=cIP, GraphqlUser=csUserName, GraphqlStem=csUriStem;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem startswith "/mock/"
| where csMethod == "GET"
| join kind=inner GraphqlPosts on $left.cIP == $right.GraphqlIP
| where TimeGenerated between (GraphqlTime .. GraphqlTime + 24h)
| project TimeGenerated, GraphqlTime, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, GraphqlStem
source:nginx @http.method:POST @http.url:*/graphql* @http.body:(*updateRESTUserRequest* AND (*text/html* OR *onerror* OR *<script* OR *javascript\:*))

| where mockTime >= graphqlTime AND mockTime <= graphqlTime + 86400
| where match(mockUA, "(?i)(Mozilla|Chrome|Firefox|Safari|Edge)")
| table graphqlTime, mockTime, src, user, url, mockUrl, mockUA
[LLM] Hoppscotch cross-team request injection via moveRequest GraphQL with null nextRequestID Exploitation Medium
Hunts GraphQL POSTs invoking the MoveTeamRequest mutation where the nextRequestID variable is null and the destCollID belongs to a team the actor is not a member of, exploiting the missing GqlCollectionTeamMemberGuard check. Targets GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v exploitation in versions <= 2026.2.1. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim operationName (MoveTeamRequest) and the precise exploit primitive the article documents — variables.next set to null while destCollID points to a victim team's collection. The article calls out that nextRequestID:null causes the backend to skip the destination team check, so the null literal is the high-fidelity signal. Detection requires HTTP body capture; Sentinel uses CommonSecurityLog.Message (the WAF body sink) and Datadog uses @http.body. EDR (Defender DeviceProcessEvents, Falcon FDR) doesn't see GraphQL payloads so those slots are intentionally empty. Cross-referenced GHSA-wj4r-hr4h-g98v. Cross-checked against: • https://intel.aikido.dev/cve/AIKIDO-2026-10461
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL contains "/graphql"
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where Message contains "MoveTeamRequest" or Message contains "moveRequest"
| where Message contains "nextRequestID" or Message contains "\"next\":null"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
source:nginx @http.method:POST @http.url:*/graphql* @http.body:(*MoveTeamRequest* OR *moveRequest*) @http.body:*destCollID* @http.body:(*"next":null* OR *nextRequestID*)
WEB
index=* (sourcetype=nginx:plus:access OR sourcetype=hoppscotch:* OR sourcetype=waf:*)
  uri_path="*/graphql*" http_method=POST
  ("MoveTeamRequest" OR "moveRequest")
  "nextRequestID" "null"
  destCollID
| rex field=_raw "\"req\"\s*:\s*\"(?<reqId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"dest\"\s*:\s*\"(?<destCollId>[^\"]+)\""
| rex field=_raw "\"next\"\s*:\s*(?<nextVal>null|\"[^\"]*\")"
| where nextVal="null"
| stats count, values(reqId) as movedRequestIds, values(destCollId) as destCollIds, dc(destCollId) as uniqueDests, earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last by src, user
| where count >= 1

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

DeviceEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Compromised litellm 1.82.7 / 1.82.8 PyPI install (TeamPCP supply-chain) Installation High
Hunts pip/uv/poetry installing the exact malicious LiteLLM versions published by TeamPCP on 2026-03-24 (online ~40 min before PyPI quarantine). Catches the initial-access moment before .pth persistence and credential harvesting fire. Rationale: Pivots on the two exact malicious version strings (1.82.7, 1.82.8) confirmed across Datadog Security Labs, Trend Micro, JFrog and the official LiteLLM security advisory. Hard-pin to pip/uv/poetry/python parents to keep noise off. [LLM] litellm_init.pth Python autoload persistence drop Installation High
Hunts the creation of `litellm_init.pth` under site-packages — TeamPCP's auto-execution mechanism that fires on every Python interpreter startup, even when LiteLLM itself is never imported. Version 1.82.8's signature persistence file. Rationale: `litellm_init.pth` is the unique persistence-file artefact called out by Datadog Security Labs, SafeDep and Sonatype — Python `.pth` autoload abuse is the differentiator vs 1.82.7 (which executes via `setup.py`). High-signal, no legitimate reuse of this filename in any clean LiteLLM release. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://safedep.io/malicious-litellm-1-82-8-analysis/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1546 T1574

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName =~ "litellm_init.pth" or TargetFilePath has "litellm_init.pth"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] WAV-disguised stager pull from TeamPCP loader 83.142.209.203:8080 Delivery High
Hunts the second-stage download where the .pth/setup.py loader pulls a binary disguised as a .wav file from 83.142.209.203:8080. Confirmed across Trend Micro, JFrog and Hunt.io as the canonical TeamPCP stager fetch. Rationale: Hunt.io and Trend Micro both call out 83.142.209.203:8080 as the stager-fetch endpoint with WAV-file masquerade — the IP+port+file-extension combination is high-fidelity and was not used outside this campaign. [LLM] TeamPCP C2 / exfil egress to models.litellm.cloud, checkmarx.zone and AS205759 nodes Command & Control High
Hunts DNS resolution or direct egress to any of the TeamPCP campaign's C2 / data-exfil endpoints: models.litellm.cloud (RSA-wrapped POST exfil), checkmarx.zone (50-min payload poll), the AdaptixC2 / Havoc backend IPs, and the trycloudflare / icp0.io rotators. These domains have no legitimate use. Rationale: All seven domains and four backend IPs are confirmed across Datadog, Hunt.io, JFrog and Sonatype as TeamPCP-exclusive infrastructure. `models.litellm.cloud` is a non-BerriAI lookalike used for AES-256/RSA-4096 POST exfil; `checkmarx.zone` is the 50-min loader-poll endpoint feeding AdaptixC2 (83.142.209.11) and Havoc (45.148.10.212). All hosted on AS205759 / Ghosty Networks bulletproof. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://hunt.io/blog/33k-exposed-litellm-teampcp-c2-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/litellm-compromised-teampcp/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/inside-litellm-supply-chain-compromise.html

[LLM] Linux user-systemd sysmon persistence drop (~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py + sysmon.service) Installation High
Hunts the Linux-side persistence artefacts dropped by malicious LiteLLM: a Python implant at `~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py` registered as a user-systemd unit `~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service`. Name choice mimics legit Microsoft Sysmon-for-Linux but the path differs. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs and Sonatype both confirm `~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py` and the user-systemd `sysmon.service` unit as the Linux persistence pair. The legit Microsoft Sysmon-for-Linux binary lives under `/opt/sysmon` or `/usr/sbin/sysmon` (never `~/.config` and never `.py`), so the path itself is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/compromised-litellm-pypi-package-delivers-multi-stage-credential-stealer
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1036.005 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/.config/sysmon/" and FileName =~ "sysmon.py"
    or FolderPath has "/.config/systemd/user/" and FileName =~ "sysmon.service"
    or FolderPath endswith "/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py"
    or FolderPath endswith "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where TargetFilePath has "/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py" or TargetFilePath has "/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SyslogMessage has_any ("/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py","/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service","systemctl --user enable sysmon","systemctl --user start sysmon")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamPCP LiteLLM Linux User-Systemd sysmon Persistence Drop
id: 3c7d5e1f-8a02-4b9c-bf1a-5e3d7c9f2a18
description: Detects the creation of ~/.config/sysmon/sysmon.py or ~/.config/systemd/user/sysmon.service — Linux-side persistence dropped by malicious litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8.
references:

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())

[LLM] Kubernetes privileged-pod DaemonSet fan-out from compromised LiteLLM workload Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation step where the TeamPCP LiteLLM payload creates privileged pods on every node in a cluster to establish persistence and lateral movement. Pivots on K8s audit logs for create-pod/daemonset events with privileged/hostNetwork/hostPID flags and ≥3 node fan-out from a single principal. Rationale: Datadog Security Labs and Trend Micro both describe the LiteLLM 1.82.8 payload's Kubernetes module creating privileged pods on every node for persistence. The cross-node fan-out (NodesTouched ≥ 3) from one user combined with privileged/hostNetwork/hostPID flags is the article-specific signal — distinguishes from legit DaemonSets (CSI drivers, log shippers) by combining principal-novelty triage downstream. Defender and Falcon left empty because K8s control-plane audit isn't shipped to MDE/FDR in standard configs. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/litellm-compromised-pypi-teampcp-supply-chain-campaign/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/inside-litellm-supply-chain-compromise.html • https://futuresearch.ai/blog/litellm-pypi-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1610 T1611 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","patch")
| extend Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name)

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

[LLM] Outbound C2 to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 (Axios npm RAT beacon) Command & Control High
Detects any host beaconing to the Axios npm supply-chain RAT C2 infrastructure at sfrclak[.]com or IP 142.11.206.73 on TCP/8000. The C2 endpoint is unique to the plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 dropper and is the highest-fidelity post-compromise indicator across Windows, Linux, and macOS payloads. Rationale: Anchored on the C2 IOCs explicitly named in the Snyk article (sfrclak[.]com:8000 and 142.11.206.73). Corroborated by Microsoft Security Blog, GTIG (UNC1069 attribution), Unit 42, Elastic Security Labs, Datadog Security Labs, and CISA advisory. The IP/domain pair has no legitimate use and is unique to this campaign. [LLM] PowerShell masquerading as Windows Terminal at %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe (Axios RAT Windows stage) Installation High
Detects the Windows second-stage Axios RAT payload: a VBScript drops a copy of powershell.exe to C:\ProgramData\wt.exe (impersonating Windows Terminal) and launches it with execution-policy bypass and hidden-window flags. Legitimate Windows Terminal lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps or Program Files — never %PROGRAMDATA%. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim Windows-stage IOC from Table 2 of the article: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe with PowerShell masquerading as Windows Terminal and execution-policy bypass. The %PROGRAMDATA% path is the discriminator — legitimate Windows Terminal ships via the Microsoft Store and resides under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps. Corroborated by Microsoft Security Blog and StepSecurity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.huntress.com/blog/supply-chain-compromise-axios-npm-package
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1059.001 T1059.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"c:\programdata\wt.exe", @"%programdata%\wt.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and FileName =~ "wt.exe")
     or (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-ExecutionPolicy Bypass", "-ep bypass", "-WindowStyle Hidden", "-w hidden", "-nop", "-noprofile"))
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\" and FolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft\WindowsApps\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and FileName =~ "wt.exe"
    | project DeviceName, DropTime=Timestamp, DroppedBy=InitiatingProcessFileName, DroppedByCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedSHA256=SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectName = "wt.exe";
let BypassTokens = dynamic(["-ExecutionPolicy Bypass", "-ep bypass", "-WindowStyle Hidden", "-w hidden", "-nop", "-noprofile"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\wt.exe"
    | where NewProcessName has @"\ProgramData\" or CommandLine has_any (BypassTokens)
    | where NewProcessName !contains @"\WindowsApps\"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetProcessName endswith @"\wt.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith @"\wt.exe"
    | where (TargetProcessName has @"\ProgramData\" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (BypassTokens))
    | where TargetProcessName !contains @"\WindowsApps\"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Linux Python RAT orphaned via nohup python3 /tmp/ld.py (Axios npm payload) Installation High
Detects the Linux second-stage Axios RAT payload: a Python script written to /tmp/ld.py and detached from its parent shell via `nohup python3`. The exact file path and orphan-via-nohup pattern are distinctive to the plain-crypto-js dropper. Rationale: Hard-anchored on the verbatim Linux IOC from the article: '/tmp/ld.py' Python script launched via 'nohup python3' to detach as an orphan background process. The path and the nohup-orphan pattern are unique enough that single-event match is high-fidelity. Corroborated by Huntress, Elastic Security Labs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/supply-chain-compromise-axios-npm-package • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceName !endswith ".local" or 1==1  // applies to all OS; Linux sensor populates this table when MDE for Linux is deployed
| where (FileName in~ ("python3", "python", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12") and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
     or (FileName =~ "nohup" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nohup" and FileName matches regex @"^python[0-9.]*$" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath == "/tmp/" and FileName =~ "ld.py"
    | project DeviceName, DropTime=Timestamp, DroppedBy=InitiatingProcessFileName, DroppedByCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedSHA256=SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DvcOs has_any ("Linux", "linux") or ActingProcessName matches regex @"/python[0-9.]*$" or ActingProcessName endswith "/nohup"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/ld.py"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine),
  (Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Facility in ("authpriv", "auth", "daemon", "user")
    | where SyslogMessage has "/tmp/ld.py" and (SyslogMessage has "nohup" or SyslogMessage has "python")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects the Linux-stage Axios npm supply-chain RAT — a Python script dropped at /tmp/ld.py and launched via `nohup python3` to orphan it from the terminal session that spawned it.
references:

[LLM] macOS Axios RAT daemon spoof + ad-hoc codesign of hidden /private/tmp binary Installation High
Detects the macOS Axios RAT payload: the dropper writes a binary to /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond (impersonating an Apple background daemon) and, for follow-on `peinject` payloads, performs ad-hoc code signing on hidden binaries under /private/tmp (e.g. /private/tmp/.XXXXXX) with `codesign --force --deep --sign -` to bypass Gatekeeper. Rationale: Anchored on three verbatim macOS IOCs from the article body and Table 2: (1) the /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond drop path that spoofs an Apple daemon, (2) the `codesign --force --deep --sign -` ad-hoc signing primitive used to bypass Gatekeeper, and (3) the /private/tmp/.XXXXXX hidden-file staging pattern. Corroborated by Elastic Security Labs and GTIG (UNC1069). Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/axios-npm-package-compromised.html
ATT&CKT1036.004 T1553.002 T1564.001 T1059.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
let RatPath = "/Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has "/Library/Caches/" and FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "codesign"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "--force" and ProcessCommandLine has "--deep" and ProcessCommandLine has "--sign -"
    | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/private/tmp/\.[A-Za-z0-9]{4,}"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "osascript" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node", "npm", "yarn", "pnpm", "bun", "sh", "bash", "zsh")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "curl" or ProcessCommandLine has "/Library/Caches/" or ProcessCommandLine has "sfrclak"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFilePath has "/Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, DvcAction),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName endswith "/codesign"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--force" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--deep" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--sign -"
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/private/tmp/\.[A-Za-z0-9]{4,}"
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] npm/node postinstall hook spawning interpreter and reaching new C2 host (Axios-style dropper) Delivery Medium
Hunts the supply-chain-dropper pattern made famous by Axios/plain-crypto-js: node.exe (or node on Linux/macOS) invoked as a postinstall hook spawns a script interpreter (wscript / cscript / osascript / python / sh) that within 60s establishes an outbound TCP connection to a never-before-seen public host. Catches the technique even if the IOCs rotate. Rationale: Generalises the dropper signature described in the article — npm postinstall hook (`"postinstall": "node setup.js"`) → node.exe → script interpreter / curl / nohup → outbound to attacker C2. The `node parent + scripting child + outbound to never-seen public host within 60s` chain is the structural fingerprint of the plain-crypto-js technique and similar npm dropper supply-chain attacks. Corroborated against GTIG / UNC1069 write-up describing the same pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sans.org/blog/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise-malicious-packages-remote-access-trojan
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1546.016

let KnownRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","registry.npm.taobao.org","npmjs.com","npmjs.org","yarnpkg.com","pnpm.io","bun.sh","jsdelivr.net","unpkg.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com"]);

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101", "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a", "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] axios npm RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 Command & Control High
Detects network egress to the campaign-exclusive C2 infrastructure used by the plain-crypto-js dropper after the compromised axios@1.14.1 / axios@0.30.4 packages execute their postinstall hook. The dropper retrieves platform-specific payloads from http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033 — any host contacting that IP or domain on any port is a near-zero-FP signal. Rationale: sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73 (port 8000, URI /6202033) are unique campaign infrastructure for the plain-crypto-js RAT dropper — they have no legitimate use. Article corroborated by StepSecurity and Socket which independently published the same C2 IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised

title: axios npm Supply Chain RAT C2 Beacon (sfrclak.com)

description: Detects network or DNS activity to the C2 infrastructure used by the plain-crypto-js dropper deployed via compromised axios@1.14.1 / axios@0.30.4 packages.

[LLM] axios RAT artifact dropped: com.apple.act.mond / wt.exe / ld.py with known SHA256 Installation High
Detects creation of the three platform-specific RAT binaries dropped by plain-crypto-js@4.2.1's postinstall hook: /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond on macOS (masqueraded as Apple ACT daemon), %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe on Windows (PowerShell copy disguised as Windows Terminal), and /tmp/ld.py on Linux. Matches on both fixed hash and path patterns so it catches renamed-but-identical samples. Rationale: Drop paths are baked into the dropper code per platform (article + StepSecurity confirm identical paths), and the SHA256s give a hash-pinned signal even if attackers rename. Sigma uses 1-of-* across selections for cross-platform single-event coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let badHashes = dynamic([
  "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a",
  "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101",
  "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where SHA256 in (badHashes)
  or (FileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond" and FolderPath has @"/Library/Caches/")
  or (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData")
  or (FileName =~ "ld.py" and FolderPath =~ "/tmp/")
  or (FileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1") and FolderPath has @"\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let badHashes = dynamic([
  "92ff08773995ebc8d55ec4b8e1a225d0d1e51efa4ef88b8849d0071230c9645a",
  "617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101",
  "fcb81618bb15edfdedfb638b4c08a2af9cac9ecfa551af135a8402bf980375cf"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (badHashes)
  or (TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.act.mond" and TargetFilePath has "/Library/Caches/")
  or (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
  or (TargetFilePath == "/tmp/ld.py")
  or (TargetFileName in~ ("6202033.vbs","6202033.ps1") and TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: axios npm RAT Drop Artifact (com.apple.act.mond / wt.exe / ld.py)
id: c2e9a5d3-8f4e-4b91-a2c6-e9f8d0b7c4e5
status: experimental
description: Detects file creation of the three cross-platform RAT artifacts dropped by plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 — matches on known SHA256 hashes and the article's specific drop paths.

      - '617b67a8e1210e4fc87c92d1d1da45a2f311c08d26e89b12307cf583c900d101'
